dimensions.name: Business judgment
dimensions.exercise: Write a one-page decision brief for a recurring report: decision owner, action, target metric, guardrails, and what evidence would change the decision.
dimensions.extension: Ask two stakeholders to independently interpret your decision brief. Resolve where their proposed actions differ.

dimensions.name: Modeling and architecture
dimensions.exercise: Sketch the grain of three related datasets. Mark join cardinalities and explain how historical attributes and freshness requirements affect the design.
dimensions.extension: Compare two viable designs using a written cost, latency, correctness, and ownership tradeoff table.

dimensions.name: Engineering workflow
dimensions.exercise: Take a transformation change through a branch and review. Include a failing regression fixture, a passing fix, and a recovery plan that preserves shared history.
dimensions.extension: Simulate a late correction and a repeated pipeline run. Demonstrate that the final result is complete and idempotent.

dimensions.name: Data trust and semantics
dimensions.exercise: Document one metric’s owner, grain, time basis, exclusions, access rules, and reconciliation checks. Have another team reproduce it from that definition.
dimensions.extension: Design a versioned migration for a metric definition, including consumer notification and a parallel comparison period.

dimensions.name: Communication and AI judgment
dimensions.exercise: Write a five-sentence decision memo: finding, evidence, uncertainty, recommended action, and the next check. Independently verify every AI-assisted claim.
dimensions.extension: Give the same evidence to a peer and compare conclusions. Identify which assumptions explain any disagreement.

questions.title: A win on the wrong metric
questions.prompt:
A checkout test randomly assigns visitors to the old or new checkout. The new checkout produces 6% more completed orders.

Before the test, the team agreed to judge success by profit per visitor, including visitors who buy nothing. Here, profit means sales revenue minus the costs of fulfilling those sales and any refunds.

The current data suggests profit per visitor is 2% lower. That is only an estimate from a limited sample. The uncertainty range runs from an 8% decrease to a 4% increase, so the true effect could be a loss or a gain.

Some refunds have not arrived yet. No agreed safety limit has been reached, and the test is allowed to continue. Leadership asks whether to launch the new checkout for everyone today. What should you recommend?

options.text: Launch it for everyone because more orders were completed. Check profit once all refunds are known.
options.reason: More orders do not necessarily mean more profit. The agreed goal includes costs and refunds.

options.text: Keep the test running within the agreed limits to gather clearer profit and refund data. Do not call it a profit improvement yet.
options.reason: The current evidence allows both a loss and a gain. More refund data and observations are needed before claiming success, and the test can safely continue within its agreed limits.

options.text: Stop the test permanently because the estimated 2% profit decrease proves the new checkout harms the business.
options.reason: The 2% decrease is an estimate, not proof of a loss. The uncertainty range also includes a possible gain.

options.text: Compare profit only among people who bought something. Leave out visitors who placed no order.
options.reason: The checkout can change who makes a purchase. Looking only at buyers changes the comparison and excludes visitors included in the agreed success measure.

questions.title: One analyst, two deadlines
questions.prompt: Sales wants a dashboard showing which customer accounts have renewed. Finance wants a renewal forecast checked against its financial records. Both are due Friday, but you only have time to deliver one. The teams also disagree about what counts as a renewal. Both say their request is an executive priority. Neither has explained what decision they will make using your work. What should you do first?

options.text: Build one dashboard with both renewal definitions and let each team choose its view.
options.reason: Two definitions may ultimately be valid, but building before establishing the decisions does not resolve the capacity conflict.

options.text: Do Finance’s work first because financial reporting should always take priority.
options.reason: The scenario gives no agreed priority rule that places Finance ahead of Sales.

options.text: Ask both teams what decision they need to make, what happens if it is delayed, and the minimum information they need. Agree the priority and owner, or take the conflict to the decision-maker.
options.reason: This makes the competing decisions and costs visible before committing scarce capacity. Escalation then has a concrete tradeoff to resolve.

options.text: Split your time equally and send both teams an early draft without resolving the different definitions.
options.reason: Equal time is not evidence of equal value and may leave both decisions unsupported.

questions.title: Revenue that grows after a join
questions.prompt: You have three tables. orders has one row per order. order_lines has one row per item in an order. payments can contain several successful payments for one order. You need a report showing the value of ordered items and the cash actually collected, grouped by the month the order was placed. Unpaid orders must remain in the report, with zero cash collected. How should you combine the tables without counting amounts more than once?

options.text: Inner join all three tables as they are, then add up the amounts by order month.
options.reason: Multiple items and multiple payments create repeated combinations. An inner join also removes unpaid orders.

options.text: Left join the item and payment rows to orders, then sum only distinct monetary amounts.
options.reason: Different items or payments can have the same value. Summing distinct amounts would incorrectly count those equal values only once.

options.text: Join the item rows to the payment rows, then divide each total by the number of joined rows.
options.reason: Items and payments may be repeated different numbers of times. A single row-count adjustment does not reliably fix both totals.

options.text: First total the items and payments separately to one row per order. Left join both totals to orders, treat missing payments as zero, then total by order month.
options.reason: Each joined table now has one row per order, so the amounts do not multiply. Left joins keep unpaid orders in the report.

questions.title: Which customer segment applied at the time?
questions.prompt: Leadership wants yesterday’s revenue grouped by the customer’s segment when each order was placed. Customers can move between segments. The source keeps a reliable history showing when each segment change took effect. The daily batch already finishes before the report is needed each morning. The team has little time to maintain extra systems. Which design should you choose first?

options.text: Keep the dated segment history and match each order to the segment that applied on its order date. Use the existing daily batch.
options.reason: The history lets you find the segment that applied at the time of each order. The existing batch already meets the deadline. Check that date ranges do not overlap.

options.text: Match every order to the customer’s current segment and save a copy of the final dashboard each month.
options.reason: Today’s segment may differ from the segment at the time of purchase. Monthly dashboard copies do not recover that missing detail.

options.text: Move all sources to real-time streaming because accurate historical reporting requires it.
options.reason: Accurate history needs the right dates and stored changes. Streaming is not required when the daily batch meets the deadline.

options.text: Update every old order with the customer’s latest segment each day.
options.reason: Replacing old segments with current ones loses the historical context the report needs.

questions.title: Fixing a change your team has already pulled
questions.prompt: A deployed Git commit changed a revenue filter and now leaves out valid revenue. It was a normal commit, not a merge commit. Two later commits contain useful, unrelated changes that do not depend on the broken filter. Teammates have already pulled the shared branch. How should you fix the problem?

options.text: Reset the shared branch to before the bad commit and force-push it.
options.reason: This rewrites history others already use and removes the later valid changes.

options.text: Revert only the bad commit on a new branch. Add a test for the missing revenue, then review and deploy the fix through the team’s incident process.
options.reason: A revert adds a new commit that undoes the bad change without rewriting shared history. The test checks that the missing revenue is restored.

options.text: Revert all three commits to return to the state before the problem.
options.reason: The later changes are independent and valid. Undoing them adds unnecessary risk.

options.text: Change the production query directly and leave the repository unchanged until the next planned release.
options.reason: The code in production would no longer match the repository. A later deployment could bring the problem back.

questions.title: A dbt model that misses corrected orders
questions.prompt: A dbt incremental model updates an orders table without rebuilding it from scratch. It uses merge with order_id as the unique key, so an incoming row can update the same order. But it only reads orders created after the newest order already in the table, using order_created_at. An order can be corrected months after it was created. The source always changes updated_at when a correction happens and makes the corrected row available promptly. How should you make sure the model picks up these corrections?

options.text: Keep the creation-date filter and add a test that order_id is never empty.
options.reason: A key check cannot recover corrected orders that the creation-date filter never reads.

options.text: Keep the filter but use both order_id and updated_at as the unique key.
options.reason: The filter still misses old corrections. A key containing updated_at would also treat different versions as different records instead of updating the same order.

options.text: Read rows using updated_at, including a short overlap with the previous run. Keep the latest row per order and merge by order_id. Test an old corrected order and check that rerunning does not create duplicates.
options.reason: The update date identifies changed orders even if they were created months ago. Overlap helps cover the run boundary, keeping the latest row avoids duplicates, and the tests check both correction and repeatability.

options.text: Read orders created in the last seven days and check that order_id values are unique afterward.
options.reason: An order created months ago is still outside this window, even if it was corrected today.

questions.title: The tests pass, but revenue drops
questions.prompt: After a source-system update, reported revenue falls by 18%. Tests confirm that the data is up to date, key values are unique, and required fields are not empty. The source now allows a new payment status called “settled”. Your report still includes only “paid”. Before telling leadership that the business has declined, what should you check?

options.text: Compare source and report totals for each status against the agreed revenue definition. Measure the excluded “settled” amounts and add a test that catches the confirmed reporting error.
options.reason: This checks whether the new status explains the difference and whether those payments should count as revenue. The business definition must guide the correction.

options.text: Rerun the freshness and uniqueness tests with stricter limits.
options.reason: These tests already passed and do not check which payment statuses should count as revenue.

options.text: Immediately count every “settled” payment as revenue because it is a valid source status.
options.reason: A status being allowed by the source does not automatically mean it belongs in revenue.

options.text: Accept the decline as real because the existing data tests passed.
options.reason: Data can be timely and complete while the report still applies the wrong business rules.

questions.title: One name, two revenue definitions
questions.prompt: Sales and Finance both report a metric called “revenue” in different BI tools. Sales uses the date an order was booked and its gross value. Finance uses the date revenue is recognized in the accounts and its net value. Both measures support valid business decisions. You are adding a semantic layer, a shared place to define metrics for reporting tools. How should you handle these two measures?

options.text: Use Finance’s formula for both dashboards and keep the name “revenue”.
options.reason: The Sales measure still supports a valid decision. Silently replacing it changes what its users are seeing.

options.text: Store both formulas in the semantic layer but keep the same display name for both.
options.reason: Putting formulas in one place does not remove confusion if different measures still have the same name.

options.text: Average the two values to create a compromise measure for the whole company.
options.reason: An average of two different business measures has no agreed meaning here.

options.text: Give each measure a clear name. Agree what it counts, which dates and exclusions apply, who owns it, and what decisions it supports. Publish both definitions and check dashboards as they switch to them.
options.reason: Clear names, definitions, and owners preserve both valid uses. Checking each dashboard during the change helps prevent unexpected differences.

questions.title: What can you honestly claim?
questions.prompt: A report shows that customers who joined a campaign spent 20% more than those who did not. But those customers also spent more before the campaign. Customers were not randomly assigned, and you do not yet have a reliable way to account for that earlier difference. Leadership wants to know whether to fund a wider campaign. Which message and next step best fit the evidence?

options.text: “The campaign increased spending by 20%.” Recommend a wider launch and put the study’s limitations in the appendix.
options.reason: The groups were different before the campaign. The 20% difference does not show how much the campaign caused.

options.text: “Participants spent more, but we do not yet know how much the campaign caused.” Recommend a limited randomized test and agree what result would justify more funding.
options.reason: This states what the data shows without claiming an unproven cause. A randomized test can give leadership better evidence for the funding decision.

options.text: “The campaign has no effect.” Stop funding because the comparison is unfair.
options.reason: An unfair comparison does not prove the campaign had no effect. It means the effect is still unclear.

options.text: “Participants spent 20% more.” Show the raw numbers without a recommendation.
options.reason: Without explaining the earlier difference between the groups, even this factual headline could mislead the funding decision.

questions.title: Checking a convincing AI answer
questions.prompt: An approved AI assistant writes SQL that runs successfully and explains why profit margin fell in a region. But it does not say how it calculated “margin”. It also joins orders directly to a customer-address table that keeps several old addresses for each customer. What should you do before sharing the explanation with leadership?

options.text: Confirm that the SQL runs and ask the same assistant how confident it is.
options.reason: SQL can run successfully while using the wrong calculation or counting an order several times.

options.text: Remove customer identifiers and share only the regional totals.
options.reason: Removing identifiers does not correct an incorrect metric or repeated amounts from the join.

options.text: Check the agreed margin definition, make sure each order matches the right historical address without being counted twice, compare totals with trusted reports, and check the evidence for the claimed cause.
options.reason: These checks address the unclear metric and the risk of repeated or wrongly assigned orders. The explanation also needs evidence that supports its claim about the cause.

options.text: Ask another AI model to rewrite the explanation and publish it if both models agree.
options.reason: Two models agreeing does not verify the metric, the join, or the reason for the decline.
